arml-2012-power-01a.title: Stay at the center
arml-2012-power-01a.body: Let the Cop search $A$ on days 1 and 2. If the Robber is not caught on day 1, he was at some $B_i$. Its only neighbour is $A$, so on day 2 he must be at $A$, and he is caught. Hence one Cop suffices: $C(M)=1$. ∎

arml-2012-power-01b.title: Parity
arml-2012-power-01b.body: Every edge joins an odd-numbered and an even-numbered hideout. Put the three Cops at $A_1,A_3,A_5$ on days 1 and 2. If the Robber escapes on day 1, he was at an even-numbered hideout; he must move along an edge, so on day 2 he is at an odd-numbered hideout and is caught. ∎

arml-2012-power-01c.title: Leave one hideout open
arml-2012-power-01c.body: Let $n=h(M)$ and choose any set $S$ of $n-1$ hideouts; the remaining hideout is $X$. Station $n-1$ Cops on $S$ on days 1 and 2. If the Robber is not caught on day 1, he was at $X$; he must move to a different (adjacent) hideout, which lies in $S$, so he is caught on day 2. Thus $C(M)\le n-1<h(M)$. ∎

arml-2012-power-02a.title: Upper bound from 1c, lower bound by "resetting"
arml-2012-power-02a.body:
By 1c, $C(M)\le6$.

Suppose only $5$ Cops are used. Fix their (deterministic) plan $S_1,S_2,\dots$, the sets searched each day. The Robber starts at any hideout not in $S_1$. Each night he is at some hideout $X$ and may move to any of the $6$ other hideouts; at most $5$ are searched the next day, so he can always move to an unsearched one. He is never caught, so $C(M)\ge6$.

**Answer: $C(M)=6$**

arml-2012-power-02b.title: Clear the map in two stages
arml-2012-power-02b.body:
**Days 1–2: search $B,E,H$.** If the Robber is at $B$, $E$ or $H$ on day 1 he is caught. If he is at $C,D$ (neighbours $B,E$) or $F,G$ (neighbours $E,H$) on day 1, then on day 2 he is at one of $B,E,H$ and is caught. So if he survives, on day 1 he was at one of $I,J,K,L,A$. Moreover on day 2 he is again among $I,J,K,L,A$: from $K$ he must go to a non-searched neighbour of $K$, i.e. $I,J,L,A$; from $I,J,L,A$ he must go to $K$ (their other neighbours $H,B$ are searched).

**Days 3–4: search $B,H,K$.** On day 3 the Robber has moved from one of $I,J,K,L,A$, whose neighbours are among $H,K,B,I,J,L,A$. If he is at $B,H,K$ he is caught. Otherwise he is at one of $I,J,L,A$ on day 3, and all their neighbours ($H,K$ or $K,B$) are searched on day 4.

So three Cops always catch the Robber within four days, and $C(M)\le3$. ∎

arml-2012-power-02b.title: Computer check
arml-2012-power-02b.body: Tracking the set of hideouts where the Robber could be (it starts as all 12; each day remove the searched hideouts, then replace the set by all neighbours of its members), a search over all strategies confirms that 3 Cops catch the Robber within 4 days, while 2 Cops never suffice.

arml-2012-power-02c.title: Bound both ways
arml-2012-power-02c.body:
By 1c, $C(\mathcal K_n)\le n-1$.

With at most $n-2$ Cops, fix their plan $S_1,S_2,\dots$. The Robber starts outside $S_1$ (possible since $|S_1|\le n-2<n$). Each night, from his hideout $X$ he can move to any of the $n-1$ other hideouts, and at most $n-2$ of them are searched the next day; he moves to an unsearched one. He is never caught. Hence $C(\mathcal K_n)\ge n-1$, so $C(\mathcal K_n)=n-1$. ∎

arml-2012-power-03.title: Sweep there and back
arml-2012-power-03.body:
**Strategy.** On days $1,\dots,n-2$ the Cop searches $A_2,A_3,\dots,A_{n-1}$; on days $n-1,\dots,2n-4$ he searches $A_{n-1},A_{n-2},\dots,A_2$. (He searches $A_{n-1}$ on two consecutive days.)

Let the Robber be at $A_R$ and the Cop at $A_C$ on a given day, and let $\Delta=R-C$. Each night $R$ changes by $\pm1$.

**Case 1: $\Delta$ even on day 1.** Since $C=2$ and $R\ge1$, $\Delta\ge-1$, so $\Delta\ge0$. During days $1,\dots,n-2$, $C$ increases by $1$ each day, so $\Delta$ changes by $0$ or $-2$ each day and stays even. On day $n-2$, $C=n-1$ and $R\le n$, so $\Delta\le1$, hence $\Delta\le0$. An even quantity that starts $\ge0$, ends $\le0$ and moves in steps of $0$ or $-2$ must equal $0$ on some day: the Robber is caught.

**Case 2: $\Delta$ odd on day 1.** Then $\Delta$ stays odd through day $n-2$ (both indices change by $\pm1$). From day $n-2$ to day $n-1$ the Cop stays at $A_{n-1}$ while $R$ changes by $\pm1$, so on day $n-1$, $\Delta$ is even; as $C=n-1$ and $R\le n$, $\Delta\le0$. From then on $C$ decreases by $1$ daily, so $\Delta$ changes by $0$ or $+2$. On day $2n-4$, $C=2$ and $R\ge1$, so $\Delta\ge-1$, i.e. $\Delta\ge0$. As before $\Delta=0$ on some day between $n-1$ and $2n-4$.

So the Robber is caught within $2n-4\le2n$ days, and $D(\mathcal P_n,1)\le2n$. ∎

(For $n=3$ the strategy is "search $A_2$ twice". A computer search shows $2n-4$ is exactly the capture time for small $n$.)

arml-2012-power-04a.title: One Cop guards, one Cop sweeps
arml-2012-power-04a.body:
**One Cop is not enough.** Fix the Cop's plan $s_1,s_2,\dots$. The Robber starts at a hideout $\ne s_1$. Each night his current hideout has two distinct neighbours (as $n\ge3$), and at most one of them is $s_{t+1}$, so he moves to the other. He is never caught.

**Two Cops suffice.** Cop 1 searches $A_1$ every day. Then the Robber can never step onto $A_1$ without being caught, so effectively he lives on the path $A_2,A_3,\dots,A_n$. If $n\ge4$, this is $\mathcal P_{n-1}$ with $n-1\ge3$, and Cop 2 runs the path strategy of problem 3 on it (a Robber who steps onto $A_1$ is caught anyway). If $n=3$, Cop 2 searches $A_2$ on two days: a Robber at $A_3$ on day 1 must move to $A_1$ or $A_2$ on day 2.

Hence $C(\mathcal C_n)=2$.

**Answer: 2**

arml-2012-power-04b.title: Sweep, then pincers
arml-2012-power-04b.body:
**Phase 1 (days $1,\dots,n-1$).** Cop 1 searches $A_1$; Cop 2 searches $A_{t+1}$ on day $t$ (so $A_2,\dots,A_n$). Let the Robber be at $A_R$ and Cop 2 at $A_C$; a Robber who ever enters $A_1$ is caught, so we may assume $2\le R\le n$. As in problem 3, if $R-C$ is even on day 1, then $R-C\ge0$ initially, changes by $0$ or $-2$ daily, and is $\le0$ on day $n-1$ (when $C=n$), so he is caught. Otherwise $R-C$ stays odd: on day $n-1$ the Robber is at an index $R$ with $R\not\equiv n\pmod2$, $2\le R\le n-1$.

**Phase 2: one adjustment day (day $n$), then pincers.**

- *$n$ odd.* On day $n-1$, $R$ is even. On day $n$ both Cops search $A_1$ and $A_n$ again; the Robber moves to an odd index, and if he isn't caught, $3\le R\le n-2$. Now the Cops are at $L=1$, $U=n$, both of the Robber's parity, and he lies strictly between them.
- *$n$ even.* On day $n-1$, $R$ is odd with $3\le R\le n-1$. On day $n$ Cop 1 searches $A_2$ and Cop 2 searches $A_n$ again; the Robber moves to an even index, and if he isn't caught, $4\le R\le n-2$. Now $L=2$, $U=n$, again of the Robber's parity, with $L<R<U$.

From then on, Cop 1 moves up ($L$ increases by 1 daily) and Cop 2 moves down ($U$ decreases by 1 daily). The Robber cannot jump over a Cop: $R-L$ and $U-R$ stay even, and each changes by $0$ or $-2$ per day, so neither can become negative without first being $0$ (capture). Since $U-L$ decreases by $2$ each day, within $\frac{U-L}{2}$ more days the Robber is caught.

**Count.** $n$ odd: $(n-1)+1+\frac{n-1}2=\frac{3n-1}2$ days. $n$ even: $(n-1)+1+\frac{n-2}2=\frac{3n-2}2$ days. Both are less than $\frac{3n}2$. ∎

(A computer search shows the true values are smaller still, for $3\le n\le9$ it is $n-1$ for odd $n$ and $n-2$ for even $n$, but the bound asked for is $<\frac{3n}2$.)

arml-2012-power-05.title: Strategies and lower bounds
arml-2012-power-05.body:
For a plan $S_1,S_2,\dots$ (sets searched each day), let $P_t$ be the set of hideouts where an uncaught Robber could be on day $t$ before the search: $P_1$ is everything, and $P_{t+1}$ is the set of neighbours of hideouts in $P_t\setminus S_t$. Capture is guaranteed on day $t$ exactly when $P_t\subseteq S_t$.

**Complete map on 7 hideouts: $W=7$.** Searching all seven on day 1 uses 7 workdays. Conversely, if $P_t\setminus S_t$ has at least two hideouts, every hideout is adjacent to one of them, so $P_{t+1}$ is everything again. Hence on the first day $t$ with $|P_t\setminus S_t|\le1$ we have $P_t$ = everything and $|S_t|\ge6$. If $|S_t|=7$ that day alone costs 7. If $|S_t|=6$ the Robber may still be at the unsearched hideout, so at least one more search is needed: total $\ge7$.

**Twelve-hideout map: $W=8$.** *Strategy:* search $B,E,H,K$ on days 1 and 2. A Robber not caught on day 1 is at a non-corner hideout, all of whose neighbours are corners, so he is caught on day 2. That is $8$ workdays.

*Lower bound* (oscillating Robbers): take the four disjoint edges $B$–$C$, $E$–$F$, $H$–$I$, $K$–$L$.

**A useful lemma (oscillating Robbers).** If $u,v$ are adjacent hideouts, consider the two Robbers who shuttle $u,v,u,v,\dots$ and $v,u,v,u,\dots$. On any given day, a search of one hideout catches at most one of them, and only if that hideout is $u$ or $v$. So a strategy that guarantees capture must make at least $2$ searches of hideouts in $\{u,v\}$ (over all days). If $M$ contains $m$ pairwise disjoint edges, every guaranteed-capture strategy uses at least $2m$ Cop workdays.
So at least $2\cdot4=8$ workdays are needed, and $W=8$.

(Note that the official solution reaches $W=8$ by a longer case analysis of which hideouts are worth searching. A computer search over all strategies confirms both values.)

**Answer: $W=7$ and $W=8$.** ∎

arml-2012-power-06.title: Bounds and extreme examples
arml-2012-power-06.body:
**$W(M)\ge2$.** A strategy with a single Cop workday searches one hideout on one day; a Robber who is somewhere else that day (possible since $n\ge2$) and anywhere afterwards is never caught.

**$W(M)\le n$.** Search all $n$ hideouts on day 1.

**$W=2$ is attained** by the star $S_n$: one central hideout adjacent to $n-1$ outer hideouts, with no other edges. One Cop searching the centre on two days catches the Robber (as in 1a), so $W(S_n)\le2$, hence $=2$.

**$W=n$ is attained** by the complete map $\mathcal K_n$. Use the sets $P_t$ of possible Robber positions ($P_1$ = all hideouts; $P_{t+1}$ = all neighbours of hideouts in $P_t\setminus S_t$). If $P_t\setminus S_t$ contains at least two hideouts, every hideout is adjacent to one of them, so $P_{t+1}$ is everything. Hence on the first day $t$ when $|P_t\setminus S_t|\le1$, $P_t$ is all $n$ hideouts and $|S_t|\ge n-1$. If $|S_t|=n$, that day alone costs $n$; if $|S_t|=n-1$, the Robber may be at the remaining hideout, so at least one more search is needed. Either way the total is at least $n$, so $W(\mathcal K_n)=n$. ∎

arml-2012-power-07a.title: Cover the smaller side twice
arml-2012-power-07a.body: Since $|\mathcal A|+|\mathcal B|=n$, one side, say $\mathcal A$, has $|\mathcal A|\le n/2$. Station $|\mathcal A|$ Cops on all hideouts of $\mathcal A$ on days 1 and 2. If the Robber survives day 1, he was in $\mathcal B$; every neighbour of a hideout in $\mathcal B$ is in $\mathcal A$, so on day 2 he is in $\mathcal A$ and is caught. Hence $C(M)\le|\mathcal A|\le n/2$. ∎

arml-2012-power-07b.title: Colour by parity of distance
arml-2012-power-07b.body:
We show $M$ is bipartite; then $C(M)\le n/2$ by the previous result.

Work in each connected piece of $M$ separately (if $M$ is disconnected, take the union of the colourings below). Fix a base hideout $X$ in the piece. For every hideout $V$ in the piece, all paths from $X$ to $V$ have the same parity; put $V$ in $\mathcal A$ if that parity is even (including $V=X$, the empty path) and in $\mathcal B$ if odd.

Let $U$–$V$ be an edge, and choose a *shortest* path from $X$ to $U$, of length $d$. If $V$ lies on it, at position $i$, then $i\le d-1$, and also $d\le i+1$ (go to $V$, then take the edge to $U$), so $i=d-1$: the initial segment is a path to $V$ of length $d-1$. Otherwise, appending the edge $UV$ gives a path to $V$ of length $d+1$. Either way some path to $V$ has length of parity opposite to $d$, so $U$ and $V$ get different colours.

Thus every edge joins $\mathcal A$ to $\mathcal B$: $M$ is bipartite, and $C(M)\le n/2$. ∎

arml-2012-power-08.title: Blocks behave like a cycle
arml-2012-power-08.body:
Each block has $n/k$ hideouts. Say the Robber is "in block $j$" when he is in $\mathcal A_j$. Each night he moves to an adjacent hideout, which lies in $\mathcal A_{j-1}$ or $\mathcal A_{j+1}$. So his block index moves like a Robber on the cycle $\mathcal C_k$ (he may have fewer options, never more).

**$k\ge3$.** Take a strategy that guarantees capture on $\mathcal C_k$ with two Cops (problem 4: Cop 1 always at $A_1$; Cop 2 sweeps $A_2,\dots,A_k$ and back). Replace "a Cop searches vertex $A_j$ of $\mathcal C_k$" by "a team of $n/k$ Cops searches every hideout of $\mathcal A_j$". Every walk of block indices is a possible Robber walk on $\mathcal C_k$, which the cycle strategy catches on some day; on that day the corresponding team searches the whole block containing the Robber, so he is caught. This uses $2\cdot\frac nk$ Cops.

**$k\le2$.** Then $\frac{2n}{k}\ge n>C(M)$ by problem 1c.

Hence $C(M)\le\frac{2n}{k}$. ∎

arml-2012-power-09.title: Complete bipartite map
arml-2012-power-09.body:
Let $\mathcal A=\{A_1,\dots,A_{17}\}$, $\mathcal B=\{B_1,\dots,B_{1995}\}$ ($17+1995=2012$), and let every $A_i$ be adjacent to every $B_j$, with no other edges.

**$C(M)\le17$ and $W(M)\le34$:** 17 Cops search all of $\mathcal A$ on days 1 and 2. A Robber who survives day 1 was in $\mathcal B$ and must move into $\mathcal A$.

**$C(M)\ge17$:** with at most 16 Cops, fix their plan. The Robber starts at an unsearched hideout. Each night, if he is in $\mathcal B$ he may move to any of the 17 hideouts of $\mathcal A$, and if he is in $\mathcal A$ to any of the 1995 in $\mathcal B$; at most 16 hideouts are searched the next day, so he always has an unsearched destination. So $C(M)=17$.

**$W(M)\ge34$:** the 17 edges $A_i$–$B_i$ are pairwise disjoint. For each such edge $u$–$v$, consider the two Robbers who shuttle $u,v,u,\dots$ and $v,u,v,\dots$. On a given day, one search catches at most one of these $34$ Robbers (the one standing at that hideout that day). A strategy guaranteeing capture must catch all 34, so it uses at least 34 Cop workdays. Hence $W(M)=34$. ∎

arml-2012-power-10.title: Disjoint edges or a star
arml-2012-power-10.body:
Let $M$ have $n\ge4$ hideouts (each adjacent to at least one other).

**Case 1: $M$ has two disjoint edges** $u_1v_1$ and $u_2v_2$.

**A useful lemma (oscillating Robbers).** If $u,v$ are adjacent hideouts, consider the two Robbers who shuttle $u,v,u,v,\dots$ and $v,u,v,u,\dots$. On any given day, a search of one hideout catches at most one of them, and only if that hideout is $u$ or $v$. So a strategy that guarantees capture must make at least $2$ searches of hideouts in $\{u,v\}$ (over all days). If $M$ contains $m$ pairwise disjoint edges, every guaranteed-capture strategy uses at least $2m$ Cop workdays.
So $W(M)\ge4$.

**Case 2: every two edges share a hideout.** Pick an edge $XY$. Every other hideout $Z$ lies on some edge, which must meet $XY$, so $Z$ is adjacent to $X$ or $Y$. If some $Z_1\ne X,Y$ is adjacent to $X$ and some other $Z_2\ne X,Y$ is adjacent to $Y$, then the edges $XZ_1$ and $YZ_2$ are disjoint—impossible. Since $n\ge4$ there are at least two hideouts other than $X,Y$, so (after possibly swapping $X$ and $Y$) every hideout other than $X$ is adjacent to $X$. Finally there is no edge $UV$ with $U,V\ne X$: choosing a fourth hideout $T\notin\{X,U,V\}$, the edges $UV$ and $XT$ would be disjoint. So $M$ is a star with centre $X$, and $W(M)=2$ (search $X$ on two days; one search can never suffice).

In both cases $W(M)\ne3$, so no such map exists. ∎
